title: Infant Bleeding Cases Jump as US Parents Increasingly Refuse Vitamin K Shot
excerpt: Refusals more than doubled to 6.8% of newborns by 2025 while vitamin K deficiency bleeding nearly quadrupled, two JAMA studies find — 2.9% of unprotected babies bled within six months, versus 1.9% of protected babies.
body:
• Two studies published November 5 in JAMA and JAMA Pediatrics are the first to show US infant bleeding rates rising alongside refusals of the newborn vitamin K shot, Reuters reported.
  • The share of newborns not receiving vitamin K more than doubled, from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, in a cohort of more than 5.2 million infants; vitamin K deficiency bleeding nearly quadrupled in a second cohort of more than 11 million infants.
  • In absolute terms, 2.9% of babies who did not receive the shot had a bleeding event in their first six months, compared with 1.9% of those who did — one extra bleeding event for every 114 newborns who miss the shot.
  • What it means for you: the vitamin K injection, standard since 1961 and recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics, is a routine decision in the first hours after birth — parents can ask their hospital team about it before delivery.

Rates of life-threatening bleeding in US infants have risen sharply since 2017 as more parents refuse the protective newborn dose of vitamin K, two studies published on November 5 found, according to Reuters. The studies, in JAMA and JAMA Pediatrics, are the first to show bleeding rates increasing in step with rising refusals.

What the two studies found

Babies are not born with enough vitamin K, a nutrient that helps blood clot, and injections at birth have been standard care since 1961. In the JAMA study, Dr Kristan Scott of Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and colleagues analysed records for more than 5.2 million US infants born between 2017 and 2025. The share who did not receive a vitamin K shot rose from 3.1% in 2017 to 5.1% at the end of 2024 and 6.8% in 2025.

The second study, in JAMA Pediatrics, by Dr Steven Woolf, Dr Elizabeth Wolf and colleagues at Virginia Commonwealth University, covered more than 11 million infants aged six months and younger over the same period. The share receiving the shot fell from 97.7% to 95%, the rate of vitamin K deficiency bleeding nearly quadrupled, and there were 5,217 bleeding events in total across the period. PhillyVoice, summarising the same study, put the rise in vitamin K deficiency bleeding at 347%, to 107.4 cases per 100,000 infants. "The rate in 2025 was approximately double what it was in 2024," Woolf said, according to Reuters.

The absolute risk, in plain numbers

Relative increases can sound abstract, so the underlying rates matter. The JAMA analysis and its accompanying commentary put bleeding in the first six months at 2.9% among infants who did not receive vitamin K, compared with 1.9% among those who did — a 47% higher relative risk, and a one-percentage-point absolute difference. Babies who missed the shot also had more than twice the risk of bleeding in the brain in their first six months. The authors calculated that for every 114 newborns who do not receive the shot, one additional bleeding event occurs. Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, between one week and six months of age, carries a 30% to 60% risk of intracranial haemorrhage, which can cause seizures, permanent brain damage or death, according to the VCU researchers' summary.

"Providing vitamin K shots at birth has been the standard of care since 1961. Now we're stepping away from that and we're seeing the consequences."

— Dr Steven Woolf, Virginia Commonwealth University

Why refusals are rising — and the limits of the evidence

Both research teams are careful on causation: the studies show the two trends rising together, not proof that one caused the other, Reuters reported. The JAMA Pediatrics team linked the timing to eroding trust in public health after the COVID-19 pandemic, rising vaccine hesitancy and growing parental scepticism about newborn interventions — vitamin K is a prophylactic injection, not a vaccine, as PhillyVoice noted. A separate Truveta analysis for Reuters of more than 1 million births found refusals accelerated further in the first half of 2026, jumping by more than 57% from January through June.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention does not track vitamin K refusals or bleeding rates, Reuters reported, which is why these record-based studies are the first national picture. In June, Representative Kim Schrier of Washington and Senator Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland called on the CDC to start tracking the events. For new parents in the diaspora, the actionable point is simple: vitamin K is discussed in the delivery room, often amid everything else happening at birth. Asking your obstetric or paediatric team about it in advance — what it prevents, and what the numbers above show — turns a rushed decision into an informed one.
